thesis.problem: Fusion power has been a laboratory result for decades rather than a product, because the machines that confine a plasma hot enough to fuse are either unstable or impossible to run continuously. The tokamak, the design most money has gone into, needs a current driven through the plasma and tends to disrupt; the stellarator is inherently steadier but its twisted magnets were long considered too hard to design and build.
thesis.solution: Proxima Fusion is the first spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, where the world's largest stellarator, Wendelstein 7-X, was built. It uses simulation and high-temperature superconducting magnets to make that design manufacturable, and is building Alpha, a net-energy demonstrator near Munich, as the step before a commercial plant.

disputed.note: Two allowlisted publications put this round at different valuations on the same day. Proxima's own announcement and EU-Startups give €2.4bn; Sifted gives €2.5bn. The register publishes the company's own figure and records Sifted's beside it rather than picking one silently — nothing in either account explains the €100m gap.

sources.title: Proxima Fusion Raises €411 Million to Build Europe’s Commercial Fusion Champion
sources.quote: Munich, Oxford, Zurich (Europe), July 7, 2026 – Proxima Fusion today announced a €411 million ($468 million) financing round, bringing the company’s valuation to €2.4 billion ($2.7 billion) and establishing Proxima as the best-funded fusion company in Europe.

sources.title: Google backs Proxima Fusion in €411m raise
sources.quote: Munich-headquartered Proxima Fusion has raised €411m at a €2.5bn valuation in a round led by XTX Ventures and East X Ventures.

sources.title: Proxima Fusion joins the club of well-funded nuclear contenders with €130M Series A
sources.quote: Most fusion companies that have raised over $100 million are based in the United States. Not Proxima Fusion, a German startup that has just secured a €130 million Series A round of funding (approximately $148 million) led by Balderton Capital and Cherry Ventures.
